title: Communicating, listening and giving feedback
moduleTitle: Shared: Growing and managing a team
audience: Team leaders who brief crews, take in concerns and give day-to-day feedback on the work.
learningOutcomes: Brief a crew on plans and reasons so that people can repeat them accurately.
Ask questions that draw out what a worker thinks before giving a view.
Give specific, timely feedback that describes the work, not the person.

instruction.heading: Communicating more than feels necessary
instruction.body: A new or changed plan is easily misunderstood when people are working in different rooms. Tell the crew what the goal is, what is changing, why it is changing and who to ask. Repeat the key points at the start of each shift. When a lead thinks a message has been said enough, it is often just starting to land with the people who were not in the room.

instruction.heading: Listening and asking questions
instruction.body: Hear out many kinds of people, rather than only the ones who side with your view. When someone raises a concern, ask why they see it that way before deciding what to do. If the same concern comes up from several people, treat it as a signal worth checking, even if it sounds minor. Asking questions also shows that the lead values the crew's view, which makes people more willing to speak up about a problem early.

instruction.heading: Feedback that helps
instruction.body: Feedback works best when it is close in time to the event, specific about the action, and about the work rather than the person. Describe what was seen, say what standard applies, and ask the worker what got in the way. Finish with the next step and a time to check. Praise should be just as specific, so the worker knows exactly what to repeat.

procedure: Before a shift, state the plan, the reason for any change and who to ask about each job.
Ask each worker one question about the plan and note any concern they raise.
When feedback is needed, observe the specific action first and write it down.
Describe the action, the standard it did not meet and the effect on the job.
Ask the worker what made the task hard, then agree one next step.
Set a time to check the agreed step and record the outcome.

workedExamples.situation: A residential crew lead notices a worker skipping the bathroom grout check on every job, but the worker has not raised any problem.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should the lead say in the feedback conversation, and what question should come first?
workedExamples.reasoning: The lead asks what makes the check hard to finish in the time, describes the missed step and the standard, and agrees a next step such as a shared check on the next two jobs. The feedback is about the action, not the worker's character.

equipmentAndPpe: A shift briefing sheet or notebook. Standard PPE on site.

commonErrors.error: Assuming a message has landed because it was said once.
commonErrors.prevention: Repeat key points at the start of each shift and ask people to say back the plan.

commonErrors.error: Giving feedback days after the event.
commonErrors.prevention: Give feedback at the next natural break, while the detail is fresh.

commonErrors.error: Describing a worker as careless or lazy.
commonErrors.prevention: Describe the observed action and the standard it did not meet.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Feedback that touches on conduct, safety breaches or complaints may need to follow the business's procedure.

qualityStandard: The lead can state the shift plan and the reason for each change in two sentences.
Feedback given in the lesson's exercise names one observable action, one standard and one agreed next step.
documentationEvidence: Shift briefing note with the plan and the points repeated.
Short feedback note with action, standard, next step and check date.
summary: Repeat key messages at the start of each shift and ask people to say them back.
Ask questions before deciding what a concern means.
Feedback should be timely, specific, about the work and followed by a check.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why should a lead repeat key points at the start of each shift?
options: Because the shift sheet is legally required to be read aloud at the start
Because a message said once often does not reach everyone who was not in the room
Because workers cannot read the sheet and some have poor eyesight or no time
Because repetition replaces checking and the checklist is not needed at all

knowledgeChecks.question: Which feedback opening best follows the approach in this lesson?
options: You are careless with the bathrooms, and that is why this keeps happening and the crew knows it
Everyone else finishes faster than you and the crew has noticed it for weeks now and talks about it
On the last two jobs the grout check was not completed; the standard requires it. What got in the way?
Your attitude needs to change and the crew has noticed this for weeks now and so has the client

knowledgeChecks.question: When several people raise the same concern, what should the lead do?
options: Note it, then wait until someone raises it again
Tell each person privately that they are the only one
Wait for the next formal review
Treat it as a signal worth checking, then decide
